findings.claim: The Forum Baths at Pompeii are repeatedly called a prescribed material source.
findings.truth: The prescribed bath source is the Central (Forum) Baths at Herculaneum. Option A: replace the lesson's prescribed-source focus and reconcile its evidence, questions and flashcards. Option B: retain the Pompeii baths only as clearly labelled additional context and add the prescribed Herculaneum source.
findings.evidence: OCR specification, Roman City Life prescribed visual/material sources, pp. 21–22; Pompeii Archaeological Park guide to the Forum Baths.
findings.ruling: Option B: Pompeii baths kept as labelled context; Herculaneum Central (Forum) Baths named as the prescribed source in heading, body, takeaway and flashcard.

findings.claim: The surrender signal is called missus and is made by raising the left hand.
findings.truth: The surrender signal was an upraised index finger, ad digitum. Missus means that the defeated gladiator was released.
findings.evidence: Royal Armouries, The World of the Gladiators, on ad digitum and the Pompeian graffiti marking Hilarus as missus.

findings.claim: Pliny, Letters 7.24 records a senator applauding a pantomime performer.
findings.truth: Letters 7.24 describes people applauding a freedwoman's pantomime performers to flatter her; it does not describe a senator doing so.
findings.evidence: Fetched text of Pliny, Letters 7.24 (Dickinson College Commentaries), sections 4–7.

findings.claim: Naevoleia Tyche funded a public building, and the bisellium suggests that she or her husband had civic office.
findings.truth: Naevoleia Tyche built her commemorative monument for herself, her husband and their freed slaves. Its ship represents their trade; the city awarded her husband Gaius Munatius Faustus a double-width seat for his services.
findings.evidence: Pompeii Archaeological Park, Nevoleia Tyche, including the monument's inscription and interpretation.

findings.claim: Juvenal, Satires 6 shows pantomime performers mocking the gods.
findings.truth: Satire 6 depicts the pantomime dancer Bathyllus performing Leda and attracting intense attention from elite women; it does not make the stated claim about performers mocking gods.
findings.evidence: Fetched text of Juvenal, Satire 6, lines 60–76.

findings.claim: Pliny, Letters 3.14 describes the murder of a senator's household slaves and their collective punishment.
findings.truth: Letters 3.14 describes household slaves murdering the senator Larcius Macedo. Tacitus, Annals 14.42 records collective execution after the murder of Pedanius Secundus.
findings.evidence: Fetched Pliny, Letters 3.14; Tacitus, Annals 14.42; Senatusconsultum Silanianum reference text.

findings.claim: The inscription on the Tomb of Naevoleia Tyche records public construction projects or public building donations by her.
findings.truth: The inscription says that Tyche built the monument during her life for herself, Gaius Munatius Faustus and their freed slaves. It records his public distinction, not her public-building donations.
findings.evidence: Pompeii Archaeological Park, Nevoleia Tyche, transcription and explanation of the inscription.

findings.claim: Libertus is a term for a freed person of either sex.
findings.truth: Libertus is a freedman; liberta is a freedwoman.
findings.evidence: University of Warwick, Roman Names: Freedmen and Freedwomen.

findings.claim: Roman domestic religion, compital shrines, the Lupercalia and the Saturnalia are prescribed content for this unit.
findings.truth: The OCR Roman City Life Culture topic list does not prescribe Roman religion or these festivals. Option A: replace the lesson with content from the listed Culture topics. Option B: retain it as clearly labelled non-exam enrichment, removing all claims that it is prescribed.
findings.evidence: OCR specification, Roman City Life Culture content and prescribed visual/material sources, pp. 20–22.
findings.ruling: Option B: lesson labelled as non-prescribed enrichment; the two 'prescribed' claims removed. Not deleted.

summary: Five lessons checked. Two high-severity scope issues require editorial decisions; the remaining verified errors have surgical edits.
